corrected_claim.title: CAP models potential deaths from SNAP cuts
corrected_claim.claim: A March 19, 2026 Center for American Progress analysis modeled about 69,600 avoidable deaths by 2040 from SNAP cuts associated with expanded work requirements. This is CAP’s conditional estimate, not an observed toll or a certain forecast. Claims about Brooke Rollins, unemployment, or fraud are outside this source.

description_short: CAP modeled up to about 69,600 avoidable deaths by 2040 under expanded SNAP work requirements.
description_medium: A March 19, 2026 Center for American Progress analysis modeled about 69,600 avoidable deaths by 2040 from SNAP cuts associated with expanded work requirements. This is CAP’s conditional estimate, not an observed toll or a certain forecast. Claims about Brooke Rollins, unemployment, or fraud are outside this source.
description_long: The Center for American Progress published an analysis on March 19, 2026, estimating that SNAP cuts associated with expanded work requirements could contribute to approximately 69,600 avoidable deaths by 2040. CAP derived the projection from a modeled reduction in participation and prior research relating food assistance to mortality. The estimate is conditional on those inputs and assumptions; it is not a count of deaths that have occurred, and it should not be described as a certain forecast. The analysis attributes the projection to CAP, not to the Congressional Budget Office. This entry should stay focused on the potential long-term mortality effect modeled in that analysis. The cited article does not substantiate the separate assertions about Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, unemployment comparisons, or a SNAP fraud rate, so those claims are removed rather than attached to the mortality estimate. The source supports an attributed, qualified description of a model and its subject, while actual future outcomes remain unknown.
supported_facts: CAP estimated that SNAP cuts associated with expanded work requirements could contribute to approximately 69,600 avoidable deaths by 2040.
The figure is a model-based projection attributed to CAP, not an observed death count.
unsupported_original_claims: The cited analysis was published in July 2026 or on the stored May 30, 2026 date.
The estimated deaths are observed or certain.
The CAP article establishes claims about Brooke Rollins, unemployment, or SNAP fraud.
evidence_gap: Future mortality effects depend on model assumptions; this source does not verify the separate Rollins, unemployment, or fraud assertions, which are omitted.
notes: Narrowed to CAP’s dated, attributed projection; unrelated claims are excluded.

frozen_original.title: CAP Analysis: SNAP Coverage Losses Could Cause 70000 Deaths by 2040
frozen_original.synopsis: A July 2026 analysis by the Center for American Progress estimated that SNAP coverage losses driven by HR 1 expanded work requirements could cause 70000 deaths nationally by 2040. The finding is based on established research linking food insecurity to higher rates of heart disease, diabetes, and obesity. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins publicly celebrated the decline in SNAP participants, attributing it to a stronger economy and fraud reduction, claims contradicted by flat unemployment data and a fraud rate of only 1.6 percent in the program.

corrected_claim.title: Trump’s 77% trade-deficit claim compares selected months
corrected_claim.claim: FactCheck.org reported that Trump’s January 27, 2026 claim of a 77% trade-deficit reduction appears to compare January and October monthly figures; the White House did not confirm the calculation. Its later full-year comparison found the 2025 goods-and-services deficit was 0.2% below 2024. The monthly comparison cannot stand in for the year-over-year total.

description_short: FactCheck.org says Trump’s 77% deficit claim appears to compare two months, not the full-year result.
description_medium: FactCheck.org reported that Trump’s January 27, 2026 claim of a 77% trade-deficit reduction appears to compare January and October monthly figures; the White House did not confirm the calculation. Its later full-year comparison found the 2025 goods-and-services deficit was 0.2% below 2024. The monthly comparison cannot stand in for the year-over-year total.
description_long: On January 27, 2026, President Donald Trump said the U.S. trade deficit had fallen by 77 percent. FactCheck.org reported that the figure appears to compare the January 2025 monthly deficit of $128.8 billion with October’s $29.2 billion figure. The White House did not confirm that this was the calculation behind Trump’s statement, so the comparison should remain attributed to FactCheck.org rather than asserted as Trump’s verified method. In a later analysis using full-year data, FactCheck.org reported that the 2025 goods-and-services deficit was 0.2 percent lower than the 2024 total. These are different measures: the 77-percent figure uses selected monthly observations, while the later comparison covers each calendar year. The sources support explaining that distinction and correcting the stored November 2025 date to the January 2026 statement and February 2026 fact-checks. They do not establish that tariffs caused the full-year change, that the annual goods deficit reached the amount claimed in the original entry, or that semiconductor imports explain the result. Those claims are excluded pending separate evidence.
supported_facts: FactCheck.org says the January 27, 2026 77% claim appears to compare the January and October monthly deficits; the White House did not confirm the calculation.
FactCheck.org reported that the 2025 full-year goods-and-services deficit was 0.2% below 2024.
unsupported_original_claims: The 77% claim was made in November 2025.
The cited analyses establish tariff causation, a record $1.24 trillion goods deficit, or semiconductor imports as the cause.
The White House confirmed the monthly arithmetic.
evidence_gap: The White House did not confirm the calculation behind the 77% figure; do not attribute the comparison method to Trump as a certainty.
notes: Uses distinct attributions for the selected-month comparison and the later full-year result; no causal explanation is inferred.

frozen_original.title: Trump Lied: Tariffs Did NOT Slash Trade Deficit by 77%
frozen_original.synopsis: Throughout 2025 and into 2026, Trump made sweeping false claims about tariffs eliminating the U.S. trade deficit. In a January 2026 Iowa speech, he claimed: In one year I've slashed our gaping trade deficit by a staggering 77%. At the World Economic Forum, he repeated the claim. In February 2026, he posted in all caps: THE UNITED STATES TRADE DEFICIT HAS BEEN REDUCED BY 78% BECAUSE OF THE TARIFFS. The Commerce Department's actual data told the opposite story: the overall 2025 trade deficit fell only 0.2% from 2024. Worse, the U.S. merchandise goods deficit — the exact measure Trump's tariffs were meant to fix — hit a record $1.24 trillion in 2025, up 2% from 2024. Economists explained that Trump was cherry-picking a single anomalously low monthly figure (October 2025) against the artificially inflated January 2025 figure, when importers had stockpiled goods ahead of tariffs. FactCheck.org found that through the full 10 months Trump was president in 2025, the cumulative deficit was actually 4.1% higher than the same period in 2024. PolitiFact rated his deficit-reduction claims False. The merchandise trade deficit set a new record precisely because U.S. companies imported massive quantities of semiconductors and tech equipment to build out AI infrastructure.

corrected_claim.title: Moody’s downgrades U.S. credit rating; White House calls decision political
corrected_claim.claim: Moody’s Ratings lowered the U.S. long-term issuer rating from Aaa to Aa1 on May 16, 2025, citing fiscal deficits and rising interest costs. Reuters reported that White House communications director Steven Cheung criticized the downgrade as political. The sourced response was not a statement personally made by Trump.

description_short: Moody’s lowered the U.S. rating to Aa1 in May 2025; a White House spokesman criticized the decision.
description_medium: Moody’s Ratings lowered the U.S. long-term issuer rating from Aaa to Aa1 on May 16, 2025, citing fiscal deficits and rising interest costs. Reuters reported that White House communications director Steven Cheung criticized the downgrade as political. The sourced response was not a statement personally made by Trump.
description_long: Moody’s Ratings lowered the U.S. government’s long-term issuer rating from Aaa to Aa1 on May 16, 2025, and assigned a stable outlook. The rating agency cited successive failures to reverse large fiscal deficits and rising interest costs. Reuters reported the White House response, including communications director Steven Cheung’s criticism of the downgrade as political. The rating change and the political response are separate reported actions: Moody’s supplied the credit assessment, while Cheung spoke for the administration. The sources support describing this dispute and its date, but they do not establish that President Trump personally made the quoted criticism in the original claim. Nor does the political response show that Moody’s acted for partisan reasons or that its stated fiscal rationale was false. The corrected account therefore attributes each statement to its actual source and keeps the focus on the credit-rating change and administration response. It does not imply a default, a change in the government’s legal ability to borrow, or a direct market effect beyond what these sources report.
supported_facts: Moody’s downgraded the U.S. sovereign rating from Aaa to Aa1 on May 16, 2025.
Reuters attributes the political response to White House communications director Steven Cheung.
unsupported_original_claims: Trump personally made the specific criticism described in the original entry.
The cited reporting establishes Moody’s acted for partisan reasons.
evidence_gap: The sources identify Cheung, not Trump, as the White House speaker; the original personal attribution is removed.
notes: Retains the rating action and attributed White House criticism, without treating the criticism as evidence about Moody’s motives.

frozen_original.title: Trump Attacks Moody's After Downgrade
frozen_original.synopsis: After Moody's stripped the US of its last AAA credit rating, Trump publicly attacked the ratings agency, calling the downgrade politically motivated and dismissing the significance of the historic event. Trump had previously celebrated the economy's performance and took personal credit for market gains. His response mirrored his 2011 attacks on S&P after that downgrade. Financial analysts warned that dismissing credit warnings while the debt continued to surge compounded investor concerns.

corrected_claim.title: U.S. flight carrying third-country deportees lands in Eswatini
corrected_claim.claim: Reuters reported that DHS said a deportation flight carrying people from several countries landed in Eswatini on July 15, 2025. Eswatini later said it held five deportees in isolated prison units. The cited material supports this Eswatini episode, not claims about stranded aircraft, South Sudan, or the legality of individual removals.

description_short: DHS said a U.S. deportation flight carrying people from several countries landed in Eswatini on July 15, 2025.
description_medium: Reuters reported that DHS said a deportation flight carrying people from several countries landed in Eswatini on July 15, 2025. Eswatini later said it held five deportees in isolated prison units. The cited material supports this Eswatini episode, not claims about stranded aircraft, South Sudan, or the legality of individual removals.
description_long: Reuters reported that the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said a deportation flight carrying people from several countries landed in Eswatini on July 15, 2025. In a separate report, Reuters said Eswatini stated it was holding five deportees in isolated prison units and aimed eventually to repatriate them. Those details support an account of the Eswatini transfer and the receiving government’s reported custody statement. The original entry combines Eswatini with South Sudan, but the cited sources here document the Eswatini flight; the South Sudan episode should not be folded into this record without its own evidence. The reports attribute the account of the flight and the refusal of return by home countries to U.S. officials, rather than independently establishing the circumstances for each person. They also do not say that planes were stranded on foreign tarmacs or settle whether any transfer violated domestic or international law. The corrected description therefore identifies the date, destination, and attributed statements while leaving individual legal circumstances and later outcomes unresolved.
supported_facts: DHS said a third-country deportation flight landed in Eswatini on July 15, 2025.
Eswatini said it was holding five deportees in isolated prison units and aimed to repatriate them.
unsupported_original_claims: The cited sources establish that aircraft were stranded on foreign tarmacs.
The Eswatini sources substantiate the South Sudan transfer also named in the original title.
The sources establish the legal status of each transfer or each person’s home-country refusal independently.
evidence_gap: Only the Eswatini transfer is documented by these citations; a separate South Sudan account and case-specific legal evidence are not included.
notes: Narrowed to the cited Eswatini flight and attributed statements; removed unsupported operational and legal conclusions.

description_medium: An April 2017 Associated Press report described Eric and Donald Trump Jr. taking the helm of the Trump Organization while their father was president and considering domestic expansion. The report documents family-business leadership and plans; it does not establish that Donald Trump Jr. worked from the White House or held a government post.
description_long: An Associated Press report published in April 2017 described Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. taking the helm of the Trump Organization during their father’s presidency and considering domestic expansion. The report concerns leadership of the family business and its commercial plans while Donald Trump held federal office. The corrected entry keeps those two supported points together: the sons’ role in the organization and discussion of domestic growth. It does not claim that a proposed expansion was completed, that any specific government action benefited the company, or that either son held a formal administration position. The source also does not establish that Donald Trump Jr. worked from the White House, a claim present in related versions of the entry. Business management by the president’s relatives can raise questions about possible conflicts, but this article alone does not document a specific policy exchange or government contract. The description therefore records what the AP report says and leaves any later business results or policy effects outside the claim unless separately sourced.
supported_facts: AP reported that Eric and Donald Trump Jr. took the helm of the Trump Organization during their father’s presidency.
The report describes the company considering domestic expansion.
unsupported_original_claims: Donald Trump Jr. worked from the White House or held a formal government position.
The report establishes completed expansion, a government contract, or a policy benefit to the company.
evidence_gap: The source documents leadership and plans, not a White House work arrangement, completed expansion, or a specific government benefit.
notes: The claim is limited to the AP report’s business leadership and expansion discussion.

frozen_original.title: Don Jr. Lobbies for Trump Org Business Interests While Working from White House
frozen_original.synopsis: Throughout 2017, Donald Trump Jr. conducted dozens of international trips on behalf of the Trump Organization while simultaneously serving as an informal adviser and frequent White House visitor, blurring the line between the family's commercial interests and government operations. Reports documented that foreign governments and businesses were paying to attend Trump Organization events where Don Jr. was the featured speaker, with the implicit understanding that access to the Trump White House was being sold. The trips took place in India, the Philippines, and other countries with active business relationships with the Trump Organization, and in several cases coincided with Trump administration decisions favorable to those countries.

corrected_claim.title: Trump urges impeachment of Judge Boasberg after deportation ruling
corrected_claim.claim: On March 18, 2025, Trump called Judge James Boasberg a “radical left lunatic” and urged his impeachment after a temporary order concerning deportation flights. Chief Justice John Roberts responded that impeachment is not an appropriate response to disagreement with a judicial decision; appeal is the proper route.

description_short: Trump attacked Judge James Boasberg and urged impeachment; Chief Justice Roberts said disagreement with a ruling is not grounds for it.
description_medium: On March 18, 2025, Trump called Judge James Boasberg a “radical left lunatic” and urged his impeachment after a temporary order concerning deportation flights. Chief Justice John Roberts responded that impeachment is not an appropriate response to disagreement with a judicial decision; appeal is the proper route.
description_long: On March 18, 2025, President Donald Trump attacked U.S. District Judge James Boasberg after the judge temporarily blocked deportations under the Alien Enemies Act. Trump called Boasberg a “radical left lunatic” and urged that he be impeached. Chief Justice John Roberts responded that impeachment is not an appropriate reaction to disagreement with a judicial decision and identified the appellate process as the proper means of seeking review. The reported exchange followed a court order affecting the administration’s planned deportation flights. The corrected entry records the public statements and legal context described by Reuters. It does not establish that Trump’s statement changed the case, caused a particular outcome for people subject to removal, or was made with a specific intent to intimidate the judiciary. Nor does it imply that criticism of a judge is itself an impeachable offense. The source supports the date, wording, and Roberts’s response; claims about broader consequences or motive would require additional evidence.
supported_facts: Trump attacked Judge James Boasberg and urged impeachment on March 18, 2025.
Chief Justice John Roberts said impeachment is not an appropriate response to disagreement with a judicial decision.
unsupported_original_claims: The source establishes that Trump acted with an intimidation motive or that the statement changed the case outcome.
The source establishes consequences for every person subject to the deportation order.
evidence_gap: Motive and broader effects are not established by the cited report and are not asserted.
notes: Corrected to the date and statements Reuters reports; avoided unsourced motive and impact claims.

frozen_original.title: Trump Publicly Attacks Federal Judge as 'Radical Left Lunatic' After Court Block
frozen_original.synopsis: After a federal judge issued an injunction blocking one of his executive orders in February 2025, Trump launched a public attack on the judge via Truth Social, calling the jurist a 'radical left lunatic' and 'Obama hack.' The attacks on the judiciary echoed Trump's first term pattern of attacking judges who ruled against him. Chief Justice John Roberts issued a rare public rebuke, reiterating that judicial independence is a foundational principle of the republic. Legal scholars warned that the attacks were designed to intimidate the judiciary and delegitimize any rulings against the administration. The pattern continued as more courts blocked Trump's agenda.
